question: When two power-driven vessels are approaching each other head-on, what should each operator do?
choice_a: The faster vessel always has the right of way
choice_b: Each vessel should alter course to starboard (right) so they pass port-to-port
choice_c: Both vessels should alter course to port so they pass starboard-to-starboard
explanation: In a head-on meeting situation, the Navigation Rules direct both power-driven vessels to alter course to starboard, passing each other port side to port side, just as vehicles on a two-way road each keep to their own right.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules head-on meeting rule (Rule 14, 33 CFR 83)

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the 'stand-on' vessel that should maintain its course and speed?
choice_c: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching on its own port (left) side
choice_d: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching on its own starboard (right) side
explanation: In a crossing situation, the vessel that has the other approaching from its own port side is the stand-on vessel and should maintain course and speed, while the vessel that sees the other on its starboard side is the give-way vessel and must take early, substantial action to avoid collision.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules crossing rule (Rule 15, 33 CFR 83)

question: Under the Navigation Rules, an overtaking vessel approaching another vessel from more than 22.5 degrees abaft its beam must do what?
choice_a: Demand the slower vessel yield immediately regardless of position
choice_b: Sound five short blasts and proceed without changing course
choice_c: The overtaking vessel always has right-of-way over the vessel ahead
choice_d: Keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken, regardless of which vessel would otherwise have right-of-way
explanation: A vessel overtaking another from behind (more than 22.5 degrees abaft the beam) is always the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken until safely past, regardless of vessel type or propulsion.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules overtaking rule (Rule 13, 33 CFR 83)

question: As a general rule of thumb, when a sailing vessel under sail alone meets a power-driven vessel, which vessel is the stand-on vessel?
choice_a: The sailing vessel, since a vessel under sail alone generally has right-of-way over a power-driven vessel
choice_b: The power-driven vessel always has right-of-way over a sailing vessel
choice_d: Right-of-way is decided by vessel size alone
explanation: A vessel under sail alone (not motor-sailing) is generally the stand-on vessel over a power-driven vessel, but this general rule has exceptions such as when the sailing vessel is overtaking, or when the power vessel is restricted in ability to maneuver, not under command, or engaged in commercial fishing.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules rule regarding responsibilities between vessels (Rule 18, 33 CFR 83)

question: Which vessel generally has right-of-way over both sailing vessels and ordinary power-driven vessels: one 'not under command' or one 'restricted in ability to maneuver'?
choice_a: Personal watercraft always outrank every other vessel type
choice_b: Both vessels not under command and vessels restricted in ability to maneuver generally have right-of-way over sailing and ordinary power-driven vessels, since they cannot readily maneuver to avoid collision
choice_c: Neither type of vessel receives any special right-of-way
choice_d: Only recreational sailboats ever receive priority
explanation: Vessels not under command (unable to maneuver due to an exceptional circumstance, like an engine failure) and vessels restricted in ability to maneuver (such as one laying cable) generally rank above sailing vessels and power-driven vessels in the right-of-way hierarchy because they cannot easily get out of the way themselves.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules vessel hierarchy (Rule 18, 33 CFR 83)

question: A vessel engaged in commercial fishing with gear deployed, such as nets or trawls, generally has right-of-way over what other vessel types?
choice_a: Vessels restricted in ability to maneuver
choice_b: No other vessel; fishing vessels always yield
choice_c: Ordinary power-driven and sailing vessels, since deployed fishing gear limits the fishing vessel's ability to maneuver
explanation: A vessel actively engaged in fishing with gear deployed that restricts its maneuverability ranks above ordinary power-driven and sailing vessels in the right-of-way hierarchy, though it still ranks below vessels not under command or restricted in ability to maneuver.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules vessel hierarchy (Rule 18, 33 CFR 83)

question: What is a give-way vessel required to do when the Navigation Rules require it to yield?
choice_a: Wait until a collision is imminent before reacting
choice_b: Maintain its exact course and speed no matter what
choice_c: Sound its horn and continue on the same path
choice_d: Take early and substantial action to keep well clear of the stand-on vessel
explanation: A give-way vessel must act early and decisively, altering course or speed enough to be obviously clear to the other vessel, rather than making a small or last-minute adjustment that could be misread.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules general responsibilities (Rule 16, 33 CFR 83)

question: What must the stand-on vessel do if the give-way vessel fails to take appropriate action to avoid a collision?
choice_a: The stand-on vessel may and eventually must take whatever action is necessary to avoid collision, including departing from its own course
choice_b: The stand-on vessel must never deviate from its course under any circumstance
choice_c: The stand-on vessel should speed up to pass before the other vessel arrives
choice_d: The stand-on vessel has no further obligation once it has right-of-way
explanation: While the stand-on vessel should initially hold course and speed, it must take whatever action is necessary, including its own course change, if it becomes apparent the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action and collision cannot otherwise be avoided.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules stand-on vessel obligations (Rule 17, 33 CFR 83)

question: Do the Inland Navigation Rules apply to personal watercraft (PWC) operators in New Jersey the same way they apply to conventional powerboats?
choice_a: Navigation Rules only apply to vessels over 26 feet
choice_b: Yes -- a PWC is legally a power-driven vessel and its operator must follow the same right-of-way, sound-signal, and collision-avoidance rules as any other powerboat
choice_c: No, PWCs are exempt from all Navigation Rules
choice_d: PWCs only need to follow right-of-way rules against other PWCs
explanation: A personal watercraft is legally classified as a power-driven vessel, so its operator is bound by the same Navigation Rules on right-of-way, sound signals, and collision avoidance as any other motorized boat operator.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules applicability to PWCs; NJSP Marine Services Bureau PWC operating rules
